title.en: Indarapatra and Sulayman: The Monsters of Mindanao
title.zh: 因達拉帕特拉與蘇萊曼：民答那峨四怪

region.en: Cotabato interior, Mindanao, Philippines (symbolic pin for the tale's monster-mountains: Matutun, Bita, Gurayn)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨哥打巴托內陸（故事中瑪圖通、比塔、古瑞恩諸山之象徵定位）

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Moro: 'Mythology of Mindanao', eBook #12814

summary.en: Mindanao, once covered with water and later dotted with prosperous villages, is laid waste by four monsters: the many-limbed Kurita, the manlike Tarabusaw, the sun-darkening bird Pah, and the seven-headed bird of Mt. Gurayn. From the land of the golden sunset, King Indarapatra sends his brother Sulayman, watched over by a life-token sapling at his window. Sulayman kills Kurita and Tarabusaw but is crushed beneath the severed wing of Pah; the withered tree tells the king, who flies to Mindanao, finds the bones, and revives his brother with a jar of water from heaven. Indarapatra then kills the seven-headed bird, finds the survivors hidden in caves, marries the headman's daughter, and the sea withdraws from the land.
summary.zh: 民答那峨昔為水淹，後成樂土；四怪驟現，吞噬生民：多肢之庫瑞塔、人形之塔拉布索、遮日巨鳥巴哈，以及居古瑞恩山之七首鳥。日落金土之國的因達拉帕特拉王遣弟蘇萊曼遠征，並以窗前小樹為其命兆。蘇萊曼誅庫瑞塔、塔拉布索，卻被巴哈斷落之翼壓死；王見樹枯，飛至民答那峨，以天賜之水澆骨復活其弟。王再誅七首鳥，尋得匿於地穴之倖存者，娶酋長之女；海水遂退出陸地，低地還於人民。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Moro (Maguindanao) narrators; presented as an archival record. Death-and-resurrection cluster: the life-token tree, death under the monster's wing, and revival by heavenly water.

passages.text: A long time ago Mindanao was covered with water, and the sea extended over all the lowlands; later many people lived in the country and the highlands were dotted with villages. For years they prospered in peace, until suddenly there appeared in the land four horrible monsters which in a short time devoured every human being they could find: Kurita, a terrible creature with many limbs, whose favorite haunt was the mountain where the rattan grew; Tarabusaw, an ugly manlike creature of Mt. Matutun; an enormous bird called Pah, so large that on the wing it covered the sun and brought darkness, whose egg was as large as a house; and a fourth, a bird with seven heads that could see in all directions, whose home was Mt. Gurayn.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Mythology of Mindanao'; not verbatim.

passages.text: So great was the destruction that the news spread to the most distant lands. In the land of the golden sunset stood a city so great that to look at its many people would injure the eyes of man, and when the tidings reached its king, Indarapatra's heart filled with compassion. He called his brother Sulayman, who said, "I will go, and the land shall be avenged." The king gave him a ring and a sword, and placed a young sapling by his window, saying, "By this tree I shall know your fate, for if you live, it will live; but if you die, it will die also." Sulayman departed, neither walking nor using a boat, but went through the air and landed on the mountain where the rattan grew. Seeing no living thing in all the wasted land, he cried out, "Alas, how pitiful and dreadful is this devastation!" — and the mountain moved, and Kurita sprang out of the ground and sank its claws into his flesh. Sulayman drew his sword and cut the monster to pieces.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Mythology of Mindanao'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On Mt. Matutun he fought Tarabusaw, who broke great branches from the trees to strike at him; the battle lasted long until the monster fell exhausted and Sulayman killed him with his sword. At Mt. Bita, not a single soul was left in any home, and as he walked a sudden darkness fell over the land: the great bird Pah was descending upon him. He struck at it and cut off its wing, and the bird fell dead at his feet — but the wing fell on Sulayman, and he was crushed. At that very time King Indarapatra sat at his window and saw the little tree wither and dry up. "Alas! My brother is dead," he cried, and wept bitterly; then, filled with desire for revenge, he put on his sword and belt and started for Mindanao in search of his brother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Mythology of Mindanao'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Indarapatra too traveled through the air, and following the bones of Kurita and Tarabusaw he came to Mt. Bita, where he lifted the severed wing and beheld the bones of Sulayman with his sword by his side. His grief overwhelmed him, but looking up he saw a small jar of water by his side, sent from heaven; he poured the water over the bones, and Sulayman came to life again, declaring he had not been dead but asleep. Sulayman returned to his distant home, while Indarapatra continued to Mt. Gurayn and killed the dreadful seven-headed bird. Peace restored, he searched for any people hidden alive in the earth, and an old woman who had hidden in a hollow tree led him to a cave where the headman and his people survived. In gratitude the headman gave him his daughter — the beautiful girl he had seen at the cave's mouth — in marriage; the people came out of their hiding-places and returned to their homes, and the sea withdrew from the land and gave the lowlands to the people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Mythology of Mindanao'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Story of Bantugan and the Island That Rose from the Sea
title.zh: 班圖干傳說與海中升起的島

region.en: Rio Grande valley, Cotabato, Mindanao, Philippines
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨哥打巴托大河谷

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Moro: 'The Story of Bantugan', eBook #12814

summary.en: Bantugan, the strongest man of the Rio Grande valley, whose father was brother to the earthquake and thunder, sends his son Balatama to woo the Sultan's daughter. Balatama survives a stone-guardian's storm, cuts a great snake in two, and wins the match by producing a golden statue from his helmet that unleashes quakes and storms until the Sultan yields. A Spanish general with ten thousand ships then claims the princess; the Sultan sets the rival fleets against each other, but after three days of smoke-covered battle and a land war, Bantugan and the Spaniard agree to withdraw — and Bantugan returns and marries her. Enraged, the general destroys the Sultan's city and returns with an endless fleet; Bantugan's warship sinks in heroic battle, drawing hundreds of Spanish ships down with it, and a great palm-covered island rises from the sea at that spot, where Bantugan and his warriors live within the mountain; his wife's own sinking ship becomes the mountain of Timaco.
summary.zh: 班圖干為大河谷最強之人，其父乃地震與雷霆之兄弟。他遣子巴拉塔馬求婚於蘇丹之女；巴拉塔馬歷經石人守衛之風暴、斬巨蛇為二，並自頭盔取出金像——金像一出，地震風暴大作，蘇丹不得不允婚。此時西班牙將軍率萬艦而來索親；蘇丹令兩方互戰，三日煙火蔽天、陸戰橫屍，最後雙方協議退兵——班圖干旋即返航成婚。將軍怒而毀蘇丹之城，再率無際艦隊而來；班圖干戰艦沉沒時拖沉敵艦數百，沉沒之處自海中升起一座棕櫚之島，班圖干與戰士居於山中；其妻沉沒之船亦化為蒂馬科山。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Moro (Maguindanao) narrators; presented as an archival record. The tale is a four-passages-long episode of the Bantugan/Darangen epic cycle in colonial-era retelling; resurrection tag covers the sinking of the ship into an island where the hero and warriors live on; sacred-place tags the island of Bongos and Mt. Timaco. The tale's Spanish opponent reflects colonial-era narrative framing, retained as recorded.

passages.text: Before the Spaniards occupied Mindanao there lived in the valley of the Rio Grande a very strong man, Bantugan, whose father was the brother of the earthquake and thunder. The Sultan of the Island had a beautiful daughter whom Bantugan wished to marry, and the head men decided that Bantugan's own son, Balatama, should carry the proposal, wearing his father's arms on the long journey. On the way his courage was tried: at a wooden fence surrounding a stone in the form of a man, he drew his knife to cut it down, and the air became black as night with stones as large as houses raining down; he protected himself with his father's shield and prayed, calling on the winds from his homeland until they came and cleared the air.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Story of Bantugan'; not verbatim.

passages.text: A great snake guarded the road, declaring no one could pass, but with one stroke of his fighting knife Balatama cut it in two, throwing one piece into the sea and the other into the mountains. After many days he reached the Sultan's city with its ten harbors, one house of crystal and one of pure gold. There the courtiers set impossible bride-prices: a figure of a man or woman in pure gold, a yard floored with gold three feet thick, gifts as many as the blades of grass in the city, a stone bridge over the great river, a ship of stone, and all the cocoanuts and leaves of the Sultan's grove changed into gold. Balatama answered that his uncles would give all save the statue, which he would give himself — but first he must fetch it from his father's town. They demanded it at once, though he warned that dreadful storms, rain, and darkness would come; they only laughed, so he drew the statue from his helmet. Immediately the earth quaked, a great storm arose, and stones as large as houses rained down until the Sultan begged him to put it back, promising Bantugan the marriage with no other gifts at all save the statue of gold. On the way home Balatama was detained four months at the stone-man's fence.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Story of Bantugan'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the meantime a Spanish general, hearing that Bantugan was to marry the princess he desired for himself, prepared a great expedition, his warship followed by ten thousand other ships that filled the harbor. His brother demanded the princess for the general on pain of destruction, and the frightened Sultan set the wedding for the next full moon. When Bantugan's own expedition, its warship decorated with flags of gold, came in sight of the city, his brothers counseled waiting — but Bantugan said, "No, let us seek my son. Even though we must enter the harbor where the Spaniards are, let us continue our search," and the anchors were lifted. An aged, bent old man, kept in a dark room and tickled in the ribs to make him young again, was carried to see the ships; he recognized the flags of Bantugan's father, his own old friend, with whom he had once contracted that their children and children's children should intermarry, and he foretold great trouble since the Sultan had promised his daughter to two people. "Go aboard your ships," the Sultan told the general, "and you and Bantugan make war on each other, and the victor shall have my daughter." For three days the earth was so covered with smoke that neither could see his enemy; when the smoke rose, Bantugan's fleet was uninjured and the Spaniard's badly damaged, so they fought it out on dry land, the ground covered with dead bodies until the Sultan commanded them to stop for the women and children being killed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Story of Bantugan'; not verbatim.

passages.text: To deceive the Spaniard into leaving, it was agreed between the two that neither should marry the princess, and both sailed away; but Bantugan soon returned and married her, finding his son on the journey home. The general, turning back to take the princess by force and finding her gone, destroyed the Sultan, his city, and all its people, and sailed away to prepare an expedition to destroy Bantugan utterly. One morning Bantugan saw the enemy fleet at the mouth of the Rio Grande, numbers so great that in no direction could the horizon be seen, and his heart sank, for he knew that he and his country were doomed. Calling his headmen, he said, "My Brothers, the Christian dogs have come to destroy the land. We cannot successfully oppose them, but in the defense of the fatherland we can die." With Bantugan at the bow, the soldiers of Islam sailed forth to meet their fate. The fighting was fast and furious, and soon the great warship filled with water and sank, drawing with it hundreds of the Spanish ships. At the very spot where it sank there arose from the sea a great island, visible today, covered with bongo palms, and deep within its mountains live Bantugan and his warriors; Moro boats passing the island are scanned by his watchers, and if they carry women such as he admires, they are snatched away — which is why Moro women fear to sail near the island of Bongos. When Bantugan's wife saw that her husband was no more, she gathered the remaining warriors and set forth to avenge him; her ship also was sunk, and where it sank there arose the mountain of Timaco, where the princess still lives in the center of the mountain with her white monkeys, and on quiet days one can hear the chanting and singing of her waiting-girls high on the mountainside.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Story of Bantugan'; not verbatim.
